column4: Only one answer connects reform to erasure of fault.
The original verse and two garbled versions remain.
Some feeding imagery survives, but the comparison with respect is lost.
The answer has to demand return of ancestral land.
Using the child is different from identifying him as the future disruptor.
The fuller partial answer retains the imperial parentage.
Both accounts and their different claims are needed.
Harming the addressee is fragmentary and loses the imperative or hand.
Neither of the two partials clearly states cold after heat.
One answer recovers the speaker but loses the urgent request.
Repetition of sweet does not explain the symptom.
Correct general and direction survive in one repetitive answer. The near-reference has a polity typo.
Asking to command differs from commanding. Ju differs from Zheng.
The terse wording with the passive attaches the appointment to the emperor.
One answer recovers the victory and city but repeats and damages the clauses.
The required number of punctures is absent from two versions.
The repeated version has traces of both events but is not a well-formed modern sentence.
